newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Global accord on Internet names set for signing.
newsitem.headline: Global accord on Internet names set for signing.

text.p: Major companies, public bodies and international organisations will next week sign an accord setting up a new global structure to manage registration of addresses on the Internet, U.N. officials said on Thursday.

The accord, shaped after nearly two years of sometimes acrimonious debate in the on-line community, is aimed at ending confusion over allocation of "top-level domain names," or TLDs, the Internet's counterpart of telephone numbers.

"What we are doing is globalising the administration of a global resource," Robert Shaw of the United Nations' International Telecommunications Union (ITU) and a member of the team behind the project told a news conference.

Albert Tramposch, a legal counsellor to the U.N.'s World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) said the new structure would have a dispute settlement system to be administered by WIPO -- like the ITU, based in Geneva.

Shaw said key firms like MCI Communications Inc which carry Internet traffic as well as the French state-owned France Telecom were among 45 players in the multi-billion dollar business who would sign in Geneva on May 1.

Shaw said the new system, to replace a monopoly on registration of the three existing TLDs held by the U.S. Network Solutions Inc (NSI), should bring down prices for by introducing world-wide competition.

It would also help reduce the problem of "hijackers" who register common brand names as Internet addresses and then offer to sell them to their original users when these eventually seek to set up their own sites.

On Wednesday, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) which funded much of the original research for the Internet, said it would not be renewing its agreement with NSI to administer existing domain names when it runs out in March 1998.

Deputy Director Joseph Bordogna said the NSF was confident the Internet community would develop a new system -- and gave a strongly positive picture of the structure to be set up next week, according to Shaw.
The new accord -- a memorandum of understanding -- was drafted by an International Ad Hoc Committee (IAHC) formed last October by key Internet organisations.

These include Internet Architecture Board, the Internet Society, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, the U.S. Federal Networking Council, the ITU, the International Trademark Association and WIPO.

Under the memorandum, seven new generic TLDs would be created removing pressure from the present three -- .com, .org and net. -- and to ease the allocation of domain names according to the profile of the company or organisation opening a site.

These would include .firm for general businesses, .store for companies offering goods for sale, .arts for sites covering culture and entertainment, .info for information services, and .nom for use of a personal name.
The accord will also establish a network of registrars around the world -- initially 28 but with more to follow -- all authorised to register Internet domain names in competition with each other.
